metadata.title: Classes of problematic smartphone use and information and communication technology (ICT) self-efficacy

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study used a two-wave longitudinal design with adolescents recruited from 12 basic education schools in four cities in Central China, with Wave 1 administered in classrooms and Wave 2 administered online via WeChat groups. The manuscript does not report the use of complex survey sampling weights or replicate-weight procedures, and it does not name any weight variables (e.g., W_FSTUWT, TOTWGT) or describe weighted estimation. Because the analysis relies on latent class analysis and regression mixture modeling in Mplus, the paper does not provide guidance on how to apply survey weights for population-representative inference. For replication with ILSA-style weighting, analysts would need to confirm whether the original sampling frame supports design weights; otherwise, results should be interpreted as sample-based associations rather than nationally representative estimates.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values are not applicable because the dependent variables are latent class memberships derived from questionnaire items (problematic smartphone use and ICT self-efficacy), not cognitive achievement scores with PVs. Missing data handling is described as maximum likelihood estimation for missing item-level responses (Little & Rubin), which is consistent with model-based imputation rather than listwise deletion; however, the paper does not report the number of imputations or whether imputation uncertainty was fully propagated through all downstream mixture-model steps, which limits transparency about the exact implementation details.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Analyses used adolescents who participated in both waves and had Wave 2 indicators for PSU and ICT self-efficacy (16 PSU items and 13 ICT self-efficacy items). The initial Wave 1 sample comprised 1607 adolescents in grades 7–10, but 1275 participated in Wave 2 (retention rate 79%). An additional 332 participants who did not participate in Wave 2 were excluded because the subgroup indicators were measured in Wave 2, yielding an analytic sample of 1275 for the latent class and regression mixture modeling. Missing item-level responses in Wave 1 were handled via maximum likelihood estimation; Wave 2 missingness was limited to non-responsiveness to the online survey, with no other missing values reported.

main_findings.dataset_used: ICILS 2018 (ICT self-efficacy questionnaire), Wave 2 (April 2019–July 2020), Chinese adolescents (grades 7–10)
main_findings.target_variable: Latent class membership: PSU & ICT self-efficacy classes
main_findings.performance_metrics: Latent class analysis (LCA) selected 6 classes; class sizes: Class 1 n=265 (21%), Class 2 n=204 (16%), Class 3 n=171 (13%), Class 4 n=111 (9%), Class 5 n=196 (15%), Class 6 n=328 (26%). Regression mixture model results reported as odds ratios (OR) with p-values for class membership comparisons. Additional analysis (Latent class membership predicted by smartphone use content types (1-year earlier)): Regression mixture model (three-step ML approach) with Class 4 (well-adjusted) as reference: Entertainment content type predicted lower odds of belonging to the well-adjusted group vs multiple other classes (e.g., Class 1 vs Class 4 OR=3.09, p<0.001; Class 3 vs Class 4 OR=2.84, p<0.001; Class 6 vs Class 4 OR=2.11, p=0.003). Information-seeking predicted higher odds of belonging to the well-adjusted group (e.g., Class 1 vs Class 4 OR=0.60, p=0.034; Class 2 vs Class 4 OR=0.61, p=0.044; Class 3 vs Class 4 OR=0.51, p=0.012). Study content type predicted higher odds of belonging to the well-adjusted group vs maladjusted and medium problem–medium efficacy groups (e.g., Class 3 vs Class 4 OR=0.58, p=0.048; Class 5 vs Class 4 OR=0.57, p=0.029).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using ICILS 2018-based ICT self-efficacy questionnaire data (Wave 2) and PSU questionnaire data (Wave 2) from Chinese adolescents, the study leveraged Gender and Family socioeconomic status (SES) to model membership in latent classes combining problematic smartphone use and ICT self-efficacy, finding that male adolescents were more likely to be in the medium problem–medium efficacy group (OR=1.58, p=0.020) and also more likely in other non-well-adjusted classes, while higher SES was associated with greater likelihood of belonging to the well-adjusted group (OR=0.57, p=0.003; OR=0.54, p=0.003; OR=0.55, p=0.001 across comparisons). This indicates that socioeconomic resources and gender-related differences may shape which adolescents develop a healthier ICT profile, suggesting that interventions should be differentiated rather than one-size-fits-all.

data.outcome_summary: This longitudinal person-centered study used Wave 2 questionnaire data from Chinese adolescents (grades 7–10) to identify six latent classes combining problematic smartphone use (16-item PSU scale) and ICT self-efficacy (13-item ICILS 2018-based instrument). The analytic sample included 1,275 adolescents from four Central China cities, with Wave 1 smartphone use content types (entertainment, interpersonal, information-seeking, utility, study) measured one year earlier. The best-fitting LCA solution selected six classes, including a small well-adjusted group (9%, n=111). Using regression mixture modeling with a three-step ML approach, entertainment use predicted lower odds of belonging to the well-adjusted class (e.g., OR=3.09, p<0.001 for Class 1 vs Class 4), whereas information-seeking and study use predicted higher odds (e.g., information-seeking OR=0.60, p=0.034; study OR=0.58, p=0.048). The paper does not report survey weights and cautions against causal interpretation, so findings should be treated as predictive associations for designing differentiated digital guidance.
